sectionsContent.title: Intermolecular Forces
sectionsContent.conceptLabel: OPTIONAL — WORTH 1 POINT ON YOUR UNIT 5 TEST

concept.summary: Complete this and turn it in at test time to add 1 point to your Unit 5 test score. Polarity decides the IMFs.
keyIdeas: Hydrogen bonding: H on N, O, or F pulled to another N, O, or F. Strongest of the three IMFs.
London dispersion: every molecule. The only IMF in nonpolar ones.

sectionsContent.directions: 1) Find ΔEN for each bond (higher EN − lower EN). A bond with a difference of 0.40 or more is polar: the electrons are pulled toward one atom. 2) Look at the shape. Polar bonds arranged evenly (symmetric) cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar. If the pulls don't cancel, it is polar. 3) Circle every IMF. London dispersion is in every molecule, so circle it every time. In Part B, draw the shape and dipole arrows first. EN: H 2.20 · C 2.55 · N 3.04 · O 3.44 · F 3.98 · Cl 3.16 · I 2.66.

keyNotes: 1 point per row, 10 total: right ΔEN, right polarity, and exactly the right IMFs circled. London dispersion is circled on every row.
H without hydrogen bonding: CH₃Cl, HCl and CH₄ (H is on C or Cl). H with hydrogen bonding: H₂O, NH₃, HF (H on O, N, F).
Polar bonds can still make a nonpolar molecule: CF₄ (1.43) and CO₂ (0.89) are symmetric, so the pulls cancel. CH₃Cl has the same shape as CF₄, but one different atom makes it polar.
CH₄: C–H is 0.35, under 0.40, so nonpolar bonds and a nonpolar molecule. I₂ and N₂: same atoms, ΔEN 0.00. Slide 35: I₂ is a solid because it has many electrons (strong LDF).
HF: 1.78 is polar covalent, just under 1.80 (same call as the 4.5 sheet).

Drawings follow the 5.4 sheet: outer lone pairs may be left off; an arrow on each polar bond (C–H gets none); polar molecules get a long net arrow, nonpolar ones net = 0. Accept any clear arrow placement that points the right way.
